newsitem.title: USA: Air Force One takes Clinton to big Midwest crowds.
newsitem.headline: Air Force One takes Clinton to big Midwest crowds.

text.p: President Bill Clinton swapped his campaign train and bus for more conventional transportation -- Air Force One -- on Monday to get to big crowds in a state in the Midwestern political battleground.

Stopping first on the Labour Day holiday at De Pere, a largely Republican suburb of Green Bay, Wisconsin, he was greeted by one of the largest crowds of his nine-day, 10-state campaign swing. About 25,000 people gathered on a bank of the Fox River at Voyageur Park, where explorers Pierre Marquette and Louis Joliet landed in the 1600s.

Later, in Milwaukee, about 10,000 party-faithful union activists gathered on Lake Michigan's shore at a "Laborfest" to hear Clinton as sailboats cruised by offshore. They even cheered as they watched Air Force One fly overhead on its way into town.
Clinton, who spent four days on a train and two on a bus last week, said the crowds taught him that "the rising tide of cynicism has been replaced by a rising tide of hope and belief in America."
He urged his union backers to get out the vote and not to be overconfident, saying, "This is the beginning of the campaign, not the end."
It was the last day of a long haul that centred around his acceptance last week of the Democrats' nomination for a second four-year term at their convention in Chicago.
He was returning later to Washington, preoccupied with how to respond to Iraq's military actions against the Kurdish minority in northern Iraq.

In both stops in Wisconsin, a state Clinton won in 1992 and has a big lead in now, the president praised the work ethic in honour of Labour Day. He also stressed his education proposals, which include a national literacy campaign and up to $10,000 a year in tax breaks for college tuition.

"That is a bridge worth fighting for," he said, referring to his postconvention campaign slogan. Clinton has been saying he represents "a bridge to the future," as opposed to Republican Bob Dole's claim that he will serve as "a bridge to the past," calling America back to a time of higher moral virtues.

He also attacked Dole's proposal for an across-the-board 15 percent tax cut, saying it would deepen the federal deficit and cause interest rates on such everyday matters as credit cards and home mortgages to go up.
Clinton was heartened by a sign in the De Pere crowd, "Republicans for Clinton," telling the person holding it, "God bless you."

A sign in Milwaukee, however, touched what Republicans considered Clinton's weak spot after the sex scandal that forced the resignation of top campaign strategist Dick Morris. "To working Americans, character matters, stupid," it said.

Stopping by the Green Bay Packers' Lambeau Field, Clinton joked with players and coaches gathered in the end zone. He compared notes on the plight of being a front-runner, since the Packers are favoured to lead their NFL division.
"You're in the same position as I am. I am ahead in the polls, but here are 65 days to go. You're on the cover of Sports Illustrated, but there is a season to play," he said.

Clinton campaign aides believe that during the trip, his message got out to 75 percent of "persuadable" voters -- those who are not beholden to either party and may hold the key to the Nov. 5 election.
The aides estimated that Clinton might have been seen personally by almost half a million people on his trip.

Clinton appeared to have used it to blunt Dole's surge in the national opinion polls. After Dole received the Republican nomination, he got a "bounce" that drew him within single digits of Clinton, but recent surveys put the incumbent between 12 and 21 points ahead.
No challenger has ever overcome a lead that great this late in a U.S. presidential campaign.
